lesson.title: Substitution Method: Solving One Variable at a Time
lesson.summary: The substitution method solves a system by isolating one variable in one equation and substituting that expression into the other equation, collapsing two unknowns into one.
lesson.body:
The substitution method solves a system algebraically, without needing a graph at all. The core idea, building directly on the substitution skill of replacing a variable with an equivalent expression, is to solve one of the equations for one variable, then substitute that expression everywhere the same variable appears in the other equation. Doing this turns a two-variable problem into a one-variable equation, which can be solved using ordinary algebra, the same techniques used to solve any single linear equation. This method mirrors, in algebraic form, exactly what the graphing method does visually: both are searching for the one pair of values that satisfies every equation in the system.

This works because of a simple but powerful fact: if an equation tells you that y equals some expression in x, then y and that expression are interchangeable in any other true statement. Replacing y with its equivalent expression does not change the meaning of the second equation; it just removes y from view, leaving an equation in x alone that can be solved directly, after which the found value of x is substituted back to recover y. Nothing about the original relationship is lost in the process, only rewritten in a more convenient form that hides one variable temporarily so the other can be found first.

Consider the system y = 2x - 3 and 3x + y = 7. The first equation is already solved for y, so substitute the expression 2x - 3 directly in place of y in the second equation: 3x + (2x - 3) = 7. Combining like terms gives 5x - 3 = 7. Adding 3 to both sides gives 5x = 10, so x = 2. Substituting x = 2 back into the first equation gives y = 2(2) - 3 = 4 - 3 = 1. The candidate solution is (2, 1). Checking both originals: y = 2x - 3 becomes 1 = 2(2) - 3 = 1, which is true, and 3x + y = 7 becomes 3(2) + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7, which is also true. The solution (2, 1) is confirmed, and since these lines have different slopes, this is an independent, consistent system.

Substitution is especially efficient when a variable is already isolated, or has a coefficient of 1, since little or no extra algebra is needed before substituting. When neither equation offers an easy isolation, the elimination method covered next is often faster, though substitution will always work eventually, since any linear equation can be solved for either variable with enough steps, even if fractions appear along the way.

Substitution also reveals the same special cases discussed earlier. If the substitution step ever produces a false numerical statement, like 0 = 5, the system is inconsistent with no solution. If it produces an identity, like 0 = 0, the system is dependent, with infinitely many solutions along a single shared line, exactly the same signals that appear when using elimination, which is reassuring since it means the two algebraic methods always agree on how a system should be classified.
